paragraphs.source_en: Besides these, there are all manner of cuts: the five-bu close crop, the three-bu crop, the one-bu crop, and so on. In the end, they may even start cutting inward into the head itself, and some novelty such as a minus-one-bu crop or a minus-three-bu crop may come into fashion. At any rate, when men rack their brains over such things, I cannot tell what on earth they mean to do. To begin with, though they originally have four legs, they use only two, which is surely a pointless waste. If they walked on all fours, they could surely move more steadily; yet they insist on walking on two, while the remaining pair dangle at their sides like two gift sticks of dried cod. Judging from this, humans must be far more idle than cats, and in the emptiness of their leisure they devise these mischievous amusements. The funny thing, however, is that whenever these idlers gather together, they keep crying, “Busy, busy.” Not only that, their faces truly do look as if they were overwhelmed with busyness. Watching the way they hop about in such a fluster, I quite worry that, if things go badly, they may be eaten alive by their busyness. Some among them, when they see me, often say, “How splendid it would be if we could be as free and easy as that cat.” If you think being free and easy is so splendid, then you may do the same yourselves. No one has asked you to scurry about in such a hurry. You manufacture for yourselves more insoluble business than you can handle and then cry, “It is unbearable, unbearable”; how is that different from lighting a roaring fire yourselves and then crying, “Hot, hot”? Even we cats, if we once started thinking up twenty different ways to cut our hair like humans do, could not remain as carefree as we are today. If you truly wish to be free and easy, you had best cultivate some discipline, at least enough to wear a woolen coat through the height of summer as I do. That said, I too do feel hot. Wearing this thick woolen coat is, in truth, unbearably hot.

paragraphs.source_en: On a day this hot, my patented privilege, the afternoon nap, has become impossible. I thought, “I must do something. It has been a long time since I closely observed human society; today I shall pay a visit to their nonsense, bustle, and scrambling affairs.” Unfortunately, in this respect my master is quite close to a cat by nature. As for afternoon naps, he takes no fewer than a cat, and especially since the school summer holidays began he has done nothing that could be called proper work; however much I observe him, I find nothing worth the effort. At such a time, if Meitei were to come, his dyspeptic body might show some reaction, and for a while he might distance himself from the habits of us cats. Just as I was hoping Mr. Meitei would hurry and come, there arose from the bathroom the splashing sound of someone rinsing himself, and from time to time the fellow called out loudly to the other person, “Ah, splendid.” “This feels much better.” “One more bucket!” The voice rang through the entire house. The person who would come to my master’s house and shout so loudly, behaving with such complete disregard for manners, could of course be no one but Meitei.

paragraphs.source_en: I thought, “So he has come after all; now I shall have half a day quite nicely disposed of.” At that moment Mr. Meitei, wiping off his sweat and putting his arm into his sleeve, came striding into the parlor in his usual manner. He called out loudly, “Madam, where is Kushami?” and tossed his hat onto the matting. My master’s wife was in the room next to the parlor, lying beside her sewing box and sleeping soundly. That sudden voice set her eardrums buzzing; she woke with a start, forced open her drowsy eyes, and came into the parlor. Meitei, wearing a fine Satsuma linen robe, had seated himself wherever he pleased and was busily fanning himself.
